USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Go into the Buenos Aires G20 meeting with Xi seeking a workable truce and a framework for continued talks, while holding the scheduled January 1, 2019 escalation (List 3 rising from 10% to 25% on ~$200B) intact as our leverage. Do not pre-commit to full escalation before the meeting, and do not roll back tariffs unilaterally — any concession must be met with concrete Chinese purchases and structural commitments. If the meeting fails to produce a breakthrough, we remain comfortable standing on our tariff posture.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is a modest net negative rather than existential. US macro fundamentals remain sound — industrial production up (104.1 vs 103.4 in July), consumer sentiment ~97.5, CPI ~0.5% over the window, Fed funds at 2.20% — so the trade war has not yet bitten the US economy hard. Our position is one of initiative and leverage: we have placed Section 301 tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese imports (List 1 $34B at 25% from July 6, List 2 $16B from Aug 23, List 3 ~$200B at 10% from Sept 24, scheduled to 25% Jan 1, 2019), with a further threat over the remainder of China's exports. The genuine costs tilt the score only mildly negative: China's retaliation directly targets the US farm belt (25% tariffs on soybeans, worth ~$14B/yr and ~60% of US ag exports to China), a real domestic political drag post-midterms, and the NYT reports market volatility and GM layoffs have rattled the administration ahead of the meeting. The Nov 1 Trump-Xi call agreeing to meet at G20 signals a diplomatic window; US officials (Kudlow) frame it as seeking concessions while being 'perfectly happy to stand on tariff policies' if there is no breakthrough. The right stance is to negotiate from strength — use the imminent Jan 1 escalation as a bargaining chip rather than burn it now, and avoid escalating pre-meeting which could collapse talks. This supports hold/negotiate posture with essentially neutral action score, consistent with the low-moderate threat.
key_factors: US economy still strong (IP up, sentiment ~97.5, Fed funds 2.20%) — trade war hasn't materially hit US growth yet
US tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese imports in place; List 3 set to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019 giving leverage
China retaliation hits farm belt — soybeans ~$14B/yr, ~60% of US ag exports to China — real domestic political cost
Trump-Xi Nov 1 call agrees to G20 meeting in Buenos Aires; scheduled escalation creates a negotiating window
Midterm political pressure and market/GM-layoff anxiety raise stakes for a claimed victory at G20

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.

China should be ready to make concessions ... or the White House could impose even bigger tariffs. Kudlow: no progress unless Chinese ready to deal; Trump 'perfectly happy to stand on his tariff policies' if no breakthrough.
Stock market gyrations, rise in interest rates and GM layoffs have rattled Trump, fueling desire to emerge with something he can claim as a victory.
US industrial production index 104.07 in Nov, up from 103.36 in July (0.7% gain).
Fed funds effective rate 2.20% in Nov 2018, up from 1.91% in July.
Soybeans account for about 60% of the US's $20B agricultural exports to China; 25% duty forecast to cut US shipments at least $4.5B.
